identity.title: Quantitative Bounds for Length Generalization in Transformers

problem.claim: Determine how transformers trained on shorter sequences can generalize to much longer, unseen inputs, and quantify the training length required.

gap.claim: Prior work established eventual length generalization beyond a finite threshold but did not determine how large that threshold must be.

contributions.claim: Provides quantitative bounds on the training sequence length required for length generalization.
Analyzes length generalization across error criteria, attention precision, and one- or two-layer transformer settings.
Shows, across the analyzed scenarios, that length generalization occurs when longer-sequence behavior can be simulated by behavior on shorter training sequences.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors characterize their work as providing the first quantitative bounds on the required training length for length generalization.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that their bounds provide qualitative estimates of the training-data length required for generalization and that they verify these insights empirically.

narrative_sequence.summary: Defines length generalization as maintaining performance on much longer inputs after training on shorter sequences.
Notes that prior work showed eventual generalization after a finite training-length threshold without quantifying its size.
Studies multiple combinations of error control, attention precision, and transformer depth.
Relates generalization in all analyzed settings to simulation of longer-sequence internal behavior by shorter-sequence behavior.
Reports qualitative estimates derived from the bounds, empirical verification of their insights, and a sharper account of extrapolation mechanisms.

source_observation.claim: The abstract states a common simulation condition spanning distinct error, precision, and depth settings, while separately reporting qualitative estimates derived from its bounds and empirical verification of the insights.

lessons.interpretation: A shared mechanism can organize a theory paper across heterogeneous cases, provided its scope is explicitly bounded by the analyzed settings.
lessons.application: Frame a multi-setting theoretical study around one invariant condition, then map each theorem or experiment to that condition and label estimates versus verified findings.
lessons.exception: Avoid this framing when the proposed mechanism is only conjectured, applies to a narrow case, or lacks a clear correspondence to the reported results.

unknowns: The abstract does not state the explicit quantitative bound formulas, threshold dependence, or theorem assumptions.
Empirical verification details, datasets, metrics, numerical outcomes, and comparisons are not provided.
The scope of the simulation condition and the meaning of “all scenarios” are limited to the settings listed in the abstract.
